hook: Picture an economy where every price, including every wage, has doubled. A worker earns twice as much and pays twice as much for everything. A firm sells for twice as much and pays twice as much for labor and materials. Is anyone better off? Is any more being produced? No: the country has the same workers, machines and know-how as before. That is the long-run view of supply.

prereq.q: What does an outward shift of a production possibilities curve show?
options: The economy can produce more of both goods
The economy is using fewer resources
prereq.why: An outward PPC shift means more resources or better technology: more of both goods is possible.

prereq.q: Why does the SRAS curve slope upward?
options: Nominal wages and some prices are sticky in the short run
Households buy more when prices rise
The government raises spending when prices rise
Firms' costs rise as fast as prices
prereq.why: With sticky wages, a higher price level makes extra output profitable.

options: Real GDP when the economy is at full employment
The highest real GDP ever recorded
prereq.why: Potential (full-employment) output is the real GDP produced when unemployment is at its natural rate.

figure.caption: Left: LRAS is vertical at full-employment output YF, whatever the price level. Right: more resources or better technology shift LRAS right.

chain.cause: The price level rises and, over time, wages and input prices rise just as much
chain.effect: production is no more profitable than before
real output returns to full-employment output

chain.cause: Output is at full employment at every price level
The economy gains resources or better technology
chain.effect: YF rises: LRAS shifts right and the PPC shifts out

ideas: In the long run all wages and prices adjust, so real output is set by resources and technology, not by the price level.
Long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) is vertical at full-employment output (potential output, YF).
LRAS shifts right with more or better labor, more capital, more land and resources, or better technology; it shifts left when productive capacity is lost.
LRAS and the PPC tell the same story: when LRAS shifts right, the PPC shifts out.
Changes in spending (AD) or in the price level do not move LRAS.

misconception.wrong: If the price level keeps rising, firms will keep producing more, so a higher price level raises real output for good.
misconception.right: Higher prices raise output only while wages lag. Once wages and input prices catch up, output is back at full employment: LRAS is vertical.

summary: In the long run, nominal wages and input prices catch up with the price level, so real output depends only on resources and technology. LRAS is vertical at full-employment output, and it shifts right when the economy gains labor, capital or better technology, just as the PPC shifts out. Spending and the price level do not move it.
